articles.title_orig: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is the best coder alive, so I put it up against Claude Opus 5.5
articles.title_zh: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is the best coder alive, so I put it up against Claude Opus 5.5
articles.content_orig:
There's a bit of a pattern I've noticed with the major AI labs and the LLMs they launch. One model will be excellent at practically anything you throw at it, while the next one can be an absolute letdown. I've seen this happen with models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and even open-weight offerings from the likes of DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen.
There's one company that's been a pretty consistent disappointment, particularly when it comes to coding, though: Google. I'll explain more below, but on September 30, Google announced its latest frontier model: Gemini 4 Argon. The company made some pretty bold claims about its coding capabilities, positioning it as one of the best models for complex software engineering tasks.
Given Gemini's history of letting me down in precisely that department, I was skeptical, to say the least. Still, in the interest of giving it a fair shot, I decided to put Gemini 4 Argon up against Claude Opus 5.5 .
I've been one of the biggest advocates of Google's AI efforts. NotebookLM, for example, is still the AI tool I use most, and I could ramble on about Google's other AI experiments for hours . When it comes to coding, though, Gemini and I have a rather complicated relationship.
I've put Gemini's models up against Claude and ChatGPT multiple times for all sorts of coding tasks. This includes building Chrome extensions , recreating apps from screenshots , developing portfolio websites, and even building my dream note-taking app from scratch. While the results have varied, there's one pattern I've noticed across almost every experiment: Gemini always seems to be in a hurry to finish the job.
It rarely goes beyond the bare minimum, often leaves features unfinished, and sometimes calls a project complete before even checking whether it runs properly. In one experiment, Antigravity built a portfolio website containing just seven of my 400-plus published articles, despite being explicitly asked to include them all. In another, it handed me a note-taking app with several requested features missing and an error that prevented it from launching properly.
This isn't exclusive to one Gemini model, either! I've noticed similar shortcomings across different generations, even with higher reasoning settings enabled. Claude and ChatGPT have certainly disappointed me too, but their weaknesses tend to vary from experiment to experiment. Gemini, meanwhile, has repeatedly fallen short on both the technical implementation and the frontend experience.
I decided to put Argon to the test using an experiment I'd carried out recently, where Gemini had let me down massively. I headed to both Claude Code and Antigravity and instructed them to build me my dream note-taking app.
Whenever I do these experiments, I make it a point to keep my prompts deliberately vague rather than spelling out every single feature I'd like to see. I've found that most AI coding tools are already pretty good at following a detailed set of instructions. What I'm more interested in is seeing how well they can fill in the gaps themselves.
Given that Gemini's biggest weakness in my previous experiments has been doing little more than the bare minimum, I figured this would be the perfect way to see whether Argon was any different. I used Opus 5.5 for Claude Code on the default Medium effort setting, and Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity on Medium effort as well. After tweaking the settings of each tool a bit to ensure both could work without constantly asking me to approve commands or file changes, I let them get to work.
Right off the bat, I noticed Gemini 4 Argon taking its sweet time. It did end up completing the initial build around 20 minutes before Claude Code, but it wasn't rushing through the process. It began by checking the development environment, figuring out what technologies to use, and making decisions about how the app should be structured.
The way it interpreted my prompt caught my attention, too! I'd mentioned being a computer science student and a tech journalist, and instead of treating those details as background information, Argon seemed to build the entire app around them. It decided to create a local-first knowledge workbench with features specifically designed for research, writing, studying, and coding.
Interestingly, it didn't stop there. It came up with an infinite canvas for brainstorming, an Obsidian-like knowledge graph for connecting notes , executable code blocks for programming, spaced-repetition flashcards for studying, and even a fact-checking ledger for keeping track of claims and sources in my articles. It also included a Markdown editor with multiple viewing modes, PDF support with citation linking, and a local vault for storing notes as Markdown files.
None of these were features I'd asked for, and this was a massive step up from previous Gemini models that wouldn't even fully create what I'd explicitly asked for!
Now, everything I've discussed above was based on what Argon had told me in Antigravity. I hadn't actually used the app yet, and for all I knew, it could've been a complete disaster. It had spun up a local server with the app running, and it was finally time to see what it had built.
I've been let down far too many times by Gemini's frontend skills, so I was bracing myself for more of the same. My immediate reaction this time, though, was "wow." Yes, the interface was fairly cluttered, and there was a lot going on, but that was largely because Argon had populated the app with a ton of sample data to demonstrate its features.
Beyond that, the overall design felt surprisingly cohesive. The warm color palette, typography, and layout all worked well together, and for once, it didn't look like another generic vibe-coded app with a dark background and purple gradients.
More importantly, it actually felt like an app designed around my needs rather than a bunch of unrelated features thrown together. The writing interface had its own fact-checking ledger, the spatial canvas let me visually connect research and ideas, and there was a dedicated flashcard system for studying.
I could actually see myself using several of these features regularly.
Argon had created a dedicated Markdown vault where every note was automatically saved as an individual .md file. So, all the data was stored locally on my Mac. I particularly liked this because it meant my notes weren't locked into the app, and I could access them directly from my file system if I wanted to.
There were a couple of hiccups, though. Initially, the local vault wasn't loading properly, and I was greeted with a "Cannot GET /" error when I tried accessing it. So, I headed back to Antigravity, explained what was happening, and Argon got to work fixing it. It updated the server configuration, added a proper vault explorer, and got everything running.
Then, I ran into another issue where the main interface kept refreshing every few seconds. Again, I went back to Antigravity, and Argon figured out that the app's automatic file syncing was triggering a continuous refresh loop. It made a few changes to how the development server watched files and how notes were synced, and that resolved the issue too.
Unlike some of my previous experiences with Gemini, where I'd spend several rounds going back and forth only to end up with another broken implementation, this time it actually seemed to understand the problem and how to solve it! So, Argon 4 defintiely seems like a massive step-up on all accounts.
Now, Claude Code took a completely different approach to the exact same prompt. Claude's version was much closer to what you'd expect from a conventional note-taking app. It had a clean, minimal three-column interface, notebooks, nested tags, daily notes, tasks, a rich-text editor with slash commands, and PDF support. The design was polished, and I'd even argue that it was easier to navigate than Gemini's version at first glance.

articles.content_orig:
Ever wanted to play Crimson Desert on your Xbox Series X or Xbox Series S without buying it? You're in luck! It's been announced this week that Crimson Desert Enhanced has received a five-hour free trial on the Xbox Store.
There are no catches with this as far as we're aware - simply search for the game on your Xbox console (specifically "Crimson Desert Enhanced" and not any other version), and you should see a prompt to download the free trial.
This will remain available to download until January 7th, so you've got a couple of months to take advantage.
Who can play the trial? The trial is available to PlayStation Plus Premium and Deluxe subscribers on PlayStation, and to all players on Xbox.
If you end up really liking it, the good news is that your progress will transfer over to the main game should you choose to purchase it, although keep in mind that the trial can't be restarted over and over again.
All of this is in celebration of the new Charting the Unknown DLC, the trailer for which we'll leave at the bottom of this article. It's an absolutely massive expansion that adds a ton of content on top of the base game, and it's available for £19.99 / $24.99 on the Xbox Store as of yesterday.
As for why Crimson Desert is now called "Crimson Desert Enhanced", it's because they've added "new cutscenes and story moments, plus expanded voice-over and language support" alongside all the updates that have arrived since launch, so now is technically the best time ever to give it a go. articles.title_orig: Chipotle is leaning on new menu items to bring diners back
articles.title_zh: Chipotle is leaning on new menu items to bring diners back
articles.content_orig:
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
Shares of Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) rose 8.9% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while the S&P 500 fell 0.3%. The gain came a day after Chipotle reported its third-quarter results on October 28. Revenue came in above estimates, while adjusted earnings per share fell below them. Four of the chain’s five peers also posted smaller gains during that session. What in Chipotle’s results did news reports link to the rise?
Chipotle Topped Sales Estimates As Transactions Rose
Chipotle’s third-quarter revenue reached $3,293 million, a little above the $3,287 million analysts expected. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.27, below the $0.29 estimate. The company released its results after the market closed on Wednesday. News reports linked Thursday’s rise to same-store sales that topped estimates, as well as to the chain’s push to bring customer traffic back .
During the October 28 call, management said same-store sales increased 2.1% in the quarter and transactions rose 0.8%. It added that Pollo Asado’s return on August 31 brought in extra transactions, while Chili Lime Chips, launched the same day, got more guests to add chips.
Fresh products give buyers a reason to return; an unchanged lineup can stall. Consider Tesla, which got 98% of last quarter’s deliveries from the Model 3 and Model Y and saw deliveries fall two years in a row. Read Trefis Big Story : How Tesla Blundered .
The industry saw a pullback in the first part of October, management said, but Chipotle’s transactions have since turned positive again. Management expects fourth-quarter same-store sales to rise around 2% overall, with the growth rate reaching 3% to 4% by the end of the quarter as smoked brisket returns to the menu in November.
Margins slipped in the quarter. Management put the company’s restaurant-level margin, its own adjusted measure, at 23.3%. That figure is down 120 basis points from a year earlier.
Did Chipotle Rise With Its Restaurant Peers?
Most of Chipotle’s peers also rose, though by much less. Four of the five companies on the Trefis peer list gained during the session, leaving Restaurant Brands International as the only decline. Texas Roadhouse posted the largest advance among them at 4.7%. The consumer discretionary sector fund, XLY, rose 0.8% on a day the S&P 500 fell. Chipotle rose almost twice as much as Texas Roadhouse, so a large part of its gain was its own rather than the group’s.
Where Does Chipotle Stock Stand After The Jump?
A rise this large is rare for Chipotle. One session in the prior 365 days saw a rise at least as big. After the jump, the stock was still down 22.3% over the twelve months to October 29, compared with a 13.3% gain for the S&P 500.
Much of that fall occurred in the last three months. The shares lost 16.0% from July 31 to October 29, while the S&P 500 rose 3.3%. Chipotle closed the session at $31.28. That price sits above the stock’s 52-week closing low of $27.52 set on October 23, 2026, and remains well below the closing high of $40.87 reached on January 23, 2026.
Chipotle is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in February 2027. Same-store sales growth is the figure to watch in that report.

articles.title_orig: Opposition bloc said weighing direct PM elections to break political deadlock
articles.title_zh: Opposition bloc said weighing direct PM elections to break political deadlock
articles.content_orig:
Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections .
Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
So how could a new government be formed?
Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible.
Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls.
Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that.
On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle.
Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office.
Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged.
Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc.
Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind.
Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers.
But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar.
While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament.
Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first.
Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed.
If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out.
After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition.
If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election.
The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed.
A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.title_zh: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.
In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.
"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

articles.title_orig: Starmer tells Dublin event Europe can no longer rely on US to 'bankroll' its defence
articles.title_zh: Starmer tells Dublin event Europe can no longer rely on US to 'bankroll' its defence
articles.content_orig:
Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.
The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.
“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.
“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”
Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.
He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.
Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.
“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.
“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”
His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.
after newsletter promotion
Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.
Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.
Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.
“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.
“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

articles.title_orig: Florida woman, 75, lost $25K in a fake sweepstakes — deputies say a New York flight attendant flew in and got onto her Apple Card
articles.title_zh: Florida woman, 75, lost $25K in a fake sweepstakes — deputies say a New York flight attendant flew in and got onto her Apple Card
articles.content_orig:
A 75-year-old Florida woman thought she had won a sweepstakes. Instead, investigators say, she lost more than $25,000 in a scheme that began after a caller posing as a Publishers Clearing House representative convinced her to pay to collect her prize.
But the alleged scam didn’t stop at cash and gift cards. Investigators say a 24-year-old New York flight attendant flew to Florida, made her way to the woman’s home and gained access to her Apple Card account. She allegedly spent thousands using a card linked to the victim’s account.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
Destiny Blake of Brooklyn was arrested Oct. 23 at Miami International Airport after an international flight, according to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office . She now faces several felony charges, including organizing a scheme to defraud over $20,000 from a victim 65 or older, fraudulent use of personal identification information of a person 60 or older and grand theft over $20,000. She has since been released on a $30,000 bond.
It started with a phone call in November 2025. The voice on the other end told the 75-year-old victim that she had won a prize and needed to mail a $500 gift card to Blake at a Brooklyn address to collect her “winnings,” according to the sheriff’s office.
Around the same time as the initial call, the victim was locked out of her email account after its password was changed and the account switched to a lookalike address, investigators said.
Between Nov. 15 and Nov. 19, 2025, the woman withdrew more than $14,000 from her bank. Blake allegedly received $14,220 through cash payments and Zelle transfers.
Then, on Nov. 18, Blake used her American Airlines employee travel benefits to fly standby from New York to Daytona Beach, then took an Uber to a hotel in Palm Coast. The following morning, an Uber dropped her at the victim’s home. She left about 15 minutes later.
Investigators say Blake had become an authorized user on the woman’s Apple Card account. A family member later found a handwritten note at the home telling the victim to contact the card issuer and say Blake was her granddaughter and had permission to use the card.
From Nov. 16 to Dec. 11, investigators identified 88 transactions totaling $10,590.30. Purchases included Apple products, an eBay order delivered to Blake’s Brooklyn home, T-Mobile and Ugg purchases, salon visits and Uber rides. In total, the woman’s losses were estimated at $25,310.
Subscribe to Moneywise: Get Warren Buffett’s best investing lessons in 1 free guide
An authorized user gets their own card, but the account still belongs to the primary cardholder. That means purchases made by anyone on the account show up on the same bill — and the primary cardholder is generally responsible for paying it. Basically, you can hand someone a card without handing over responsibility for the charges.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing. For example, parents might add a teenager to help them learn how credit works or someone might give a partner or family member a card for everyday expenses. The arrangement depends on the primary cardholder being comfortable with how that person will use it.
In this case, investigators say Blake allegedly went much further, using the victim’s Apple Card to make thousands of dollars in purchases after gaining access to the account.
The woman was also allegedly given instructions on what to tell the card issuer about Blake’s relationship to her. If someone asks you to add them to your account as part of a supposed prize claim, that’s a good reason to stop and call your card issuer directly. Use the number on the back of your card or the issuer’s official website rather than the number provided by the caller.
The Federal Trade Commission also warns that legitimate sweepstakes don’t charge winners to collect a prize. If someone asks for a gift card, cash, a wire transfer or your financial information, you can be pretty confident that the prize isn’t what they say it is. In this case, the woman was asked to send a $500 gift card before the alleged scam took an even more costly turn.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's Starlink could be your next cellphone carrier
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's Starlink could be your next cellphone carrier
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump praised Elon Musk at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, recounting how the SpaceX founder rapidly deployed Starlink to hurricane-ravaged North Carolina. Trump says the technology restored critical communications and helped save hundreds of lives.
Ever look at your cellphone bill and wonder why you're paying so much when you still can't get a decent signal? Maybe calls drop inside your house or your phone loses service during a road trip. It's frustrating, especially when the big wireless companies keep promising better coverage.
Now, Elon Musk wants to give you another option. His company, SpaceX, is reportedly pursuing access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States. The goal is to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier that could compete directly with Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile. If Musk pulls this off, the way you choose your cellphone service could change.
Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay.
Elon Musk's SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites as it explores turning Starlink into a nationwide wireless carrier. (Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
SpaceX is reportedly negotiating with major cellular infrastructure companies to secure access to at least 80,000 sites nationwide. One company reportedly involved is Crown Castle, which owns and operates roughly 40,000 cell towers across the country. During an Oct. 21 earnings call, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant was asked about potential leasing discussions with SpaceX and other satellite providers. His response was revealing. "You can assume that we're talking to all parties," he said, although he declined to discuss specific customers. That's a significant development.
Cell towers provide the infrastructure that keeps our phones connected across the country. Wireless companies typically lease space on these towers rather than build every structure themselves. That approach helps them expand coverage without taking on the full cost of owning the infrastructure.
For perspective, the Wireless Infrastructure Association counted about 158,500 purpose-built cell towers nationwide in 2025. SpaceX's reported target of 80,000 cell sites would represent a substantial expansion, although cell sites and physical towers are not the same thing. A single tower can support equipment from multiple wireless networks, so the two figures are not directly comparable. Still, the reported discussions remain preliminary. SpaceX has not publicly confirmed agreements covering those 80,000 sites.
Here's something you might be wondering. If Starlink already has satellites orbiting Earth, why does SpaceX need thousands of cell towers? The answer comes down to how wireless coverage works. Satellites can provide connectivity in remote areas where traditional cell towers are scarce. However, signals from space can struggle to reach phones inside buildings or in places with an obstructed view of the sky.
That's where ground-based cellular networks come in. Traditional towers can provide stronger, more consistent service in areas where satellite connections face limitations. By combining both technologies, SpaceX hopes to create a network that keeps people connected across more locations.
There's another interesting piece to the strategy. SpaceX has also discussed adding small cellular base stations to equipment installed at Starlink customers' homes and businesses. Those stations could help provide mobile coverage without requiring the company to rely entirely on traditional cell towers.
However, there's a catch. Starlink customers install their equipment where they need home internet. Those locations may not line up with where a nationwide cellphone network needs additional coverage. That's why access to established cellular infrastructure could prove so valuable.
FCC CHAIRMAN CARR SAYS SPECTRUM AUCTION WILL MAKE WIRELESS FASTER, CHEAPER WHILE RAISING BILLIONS FOR TREASURY
SpaceX could challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile by combining Starlink's satellite technology with traditional cellphone towers across the United States. (Kirby Lee/Getty Images)
SpaceX has already made several investments that support its wireless ambitions. On October 8, investment firm Grain Management announced an agreement to sell its nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz wireless spectrum to SpaceX. The deal remains subject to Federal Communications Commission approval.
If you're unfamiliar with spectrum, think of it as the radio frequencies that carry wireless signals between your phone and a network. Different frequencies have different strengths. Lower-frequency signals generally travel farther and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency signals. That could help Starlink Mobile deliver coverage in places where satellite connections alone might struggle.
SpaceX also received FCC authorization in October to deploy a new constellation of up to 15,000 direct-to-device satellites . These satellites are designed to communicate with compatible phones and support a broader range of mobile services. However, that authorization doesn't mean all the satellites are already operating.
Together, those developments help explain why Musk is getting serious about the wireless business. SpaceX is assembling the pieces needed to connect phones through satellites and ground-based networks. During SpaceX's October earnings call, Musk said the company would expand its terrestrial networks to provide broader connectivity wherever SpaceX and Starlink are permitted to operate. He also said satellite launches and spectrum acquisitions would help Starlink Mobile become a major U.S. wireless carrier.
The possibility has already caught Wall Street's attention. Following reports of SpaceX's cell tower negotiations, shares of major wireless companies fell on October 23. Meanwhile, cellular infrastructure companies saw their shares rise as investors anticipated potential business from SpaceX. But entering the wireless market won't come cheap.
Analysts at TD Cowen reportedly estimated that building a nationwide terrestrial network could cost more than $80 billion. The process could take years, even for a company with SpaceX's financial resources. And SpaceX would face established competitors with decades of experience. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile already operate extensive networks. They also have millions of customers and established retail operations.
Interestingly, SpaceX already works with T-Mobile through its T-Satellite with Starlink service. That partnership allows compatible phones to connect to satellites in certain areas without traditional cellular coverage. So, Musk's company currently helps support a wireless provider it could eventually compete against. That's an unusual position, but it also gives SpaceX experience delivering satellite connectivity to everyday phones. If Starlink Mobile becomes a standalone carrier, customers could eventually have another nationwide option beyond today's three dominant providers.
If you're already wondering when you can switch, there's an important detail to keep in mind. SpaceX has not announced a confirmed launch date for a fully independent nationwide cellphone service. The company expects to begin deploying its next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites in 2027.

articles.title_orig: China joins global race to reawaken brain-injury patients through ultrasound therapy
articles.title_zh: China joins global race to reawaken brain-injury patients through ultrasound therapy
articles.content_orig:
Chinese researchers have reported early promising results, as scientists worldwide explore ways to restore consciousness without invasive surgery
After spending three months in a coma following a brain haemorrhage, a patient in China has regained the ability to speak, eat and walk with support – part of an early clinical trial using targeted sound waves to help “wake up” severely damaged brains, according to state media.
The technology, developed by a coalition including the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, used focused ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep within the brain without requiring invasive surgery or implanted electrodes, state broadcaster CCTV reported earlier this week.

Now that the MMORPG Final Fantasy XIV Online is available on the Switch 2, Square Enix is looking towards the game's sixth expansion, Evercold .
We previously heard how it would be coming in January 2027, and now at the Final Fantasy XIV Fan Fest in Tokyo this weekend, Square Enix has announced the date has been shifted to 23rd February 2027 . Pre-orders will begin on 4th November 2026 , with early access opening on 19th February 2027 .
As previously confirmed, it will come with new jobs, cities, areas, dungeons, trials, new areas, a level cap increase and much more. Joining the Bastion job is the new physical ranged DPS, Zephyr. You can find out more about what's included in Evercold in our previous story and on the FFXIV YouTube channel .

articles.content_orig:
As Hong Kong residents explore a wider range of mainland cities, businesses in Guangzhou, Zhongshan and Jiangmen are reaping rewards
Seventy-something Hong Kong retiree Leung Ching says a meal for four in Shenzhen, the megacity in mainland China roughly an hour’s train ride away, that cost just over 300 yuan (US$45) a few years ago now runs to 500 to 600 yuan.
It would cost around HK$1,000 (US$127.50) in Hong Kong, but only 300 yuan in Guangzhou and just 200 yuan in Zhongshan, two cities within two hours of Hong Kong.
“Shenzhen is becoming less and less affordable,” said Leung, a retired vendor.

articles.title_orig: China's Blue Bay initiative gets UN honor
articles.title_zh: China's Blue Bay initiative gets UN honor
articles.content_orig:
China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was named a 2026 United Nations World Restoration Flagship on Thursday in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia, highlighting international recognition of China's achievements in marine ecological protection and restoration.
The announcement was made at the "Restoration Day" event during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, or COP17.
Led by the Ministry of Natural Resources and the Ministry of Finance, the initiative is the second nationwide program from China to receive the honor, following the Shan-Shui Initiative, which was among the first global flagships in 2022. The achievement makes China the first country to have two nationwide actions recognized as World Restoration Flagships.
The World Restoration Flagship, jointly established by the United Nations Environment Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization, is a global recognition under the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, highlighting large-scale restoration projects that are exemplary, representative and globally influential. In this round, initiatives from Colombia, Ethiopia, Italy and the United States were also honored.
At the awarding ceremony, Raimund Jehle, deputy regional representative for Europe and Central Asia at the Food and Agriculture Organization, underscored the importance of healthy coastal ecosystems for biodiversity, food security and people's livelihoods.
"Healthy coastal ecosystems support fisheries, protect communities and strengthen resilience to climate change. Their restoration requires us to work across the boundaries between land and sea and across sectors and institutions," Jehle said.
"China's Blue Bay Initiative demonstrates the value of this integrated approach, bringing together ecological restoration, coordinated governance and public investment," he added.
Building on the experience of the Yundang Lake restoration in Xiamen, Fujian province, coastal regions across China have advanced integrated land-sea management and marine ecological restoration on a large scale.
During the 13th (2016-20) and 14th Five-Year Plan periods (2021-25), China's central government allocated 36.63 billion yuan ($5.5 billion) to coastal provinces for the implementation of 194 major marine ecological restoration projects. This led to the restoration of more than 150,000 hectares of coastal wetlands, the management of Spartina alterniflora, an invasive cordgrass species, and the rehabilitation of more than 2,000 kilometers of coastline.
Zhong Chongjun, deputy director-general of the ministry's department of territorial space ecological restoration, said the recognition demonstrates full acknowledgment from the international community of China's practical achievements in marine ecological protection and restoration.
"The 194 major marine ecological restoration projects have effectively improved the quality and stability of key marine ecosystems, raised the level of biodiversity conservation, expanded quality coastal access for the public, enhanced coastal disaster prevention and mitigation capacity, and strengthened the marine ecological security barrier," Zhong said. "Thanks to sustained efforts, China's mangrove area has increased to 31,700 hectares, making the country one of the few in the world where mangrove coverage is continuously expanding," he added.
Wang Lei, director-general of the department, described the selection as both "an honor and a responsibility".
"We will take this as a new start, continuing to implement actions for blue bays, beautiful shorelines and harmonious islands," Wang said.
He emphasized the focus on improving the quality and function of key marine ecosystems, such as mangroves, coral reefs, sea grass beds, and coastal salt marshes. The goal is to deliver more ecological restoration outcomes that enhance livelihoods, boost employment and income, and foster a new development paradigm of harmony between humanity and the sea.
"We stand ready to deepen exchanges and cooperation with all countries, share our experience, build global consensus, jointly advance the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration and work hand in hand to safeguard our blue planet," Wang said.

articles.title_orig: Britain’s Prime Minister Says He’s Open to a Formal Apology for Slavery
articles.title_zh: Britain’s Prime Minister Says He’s Open to a Formal Apology for Slavery
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to a formal apology for his country’s role in the transatlantic slave trade , but ruled out financial reparations as King Charles III continued his tour of the Caribbean.
Burnham’s comments show a marked shift in stance for the U.K.,  which has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
They came as he is due to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week. Charles, as head of the “family of nations,” will preside over the event.
“We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade,” Burnham wrote in an op-ed in The Guardian newspaper in an article published Friday. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”
But Burnham ruled out financial reparations, saying the British people of today who “played no personal part” in the slave trade could not be held liable.
The transatlantic trade in enslaved people was central to European colonialism and the growth of the British Empire , as millions of Africans were trafficked to the Americas to grow and harvest cash crops, while being subjected to violence, torture, sexual abuse and the denial of basic human rights.
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on X that he welcomed the prime minister’s openness to a formal apology.
Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also took to X where he wrote: “Open-minded dialogue is always a good place to start addressing difficult issues.”
Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal.
Caribbean nations had urged British to acknowledge its role in the salve trade ahead of Charles’ visit to the Bahamas and Guyana last week.
Charles visited Clifford Park last week where in 1973 he granted The Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule.
Members of The Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a nearby road to protest.
“Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against Black people.”
In his first public remarks on the island nation, Charles said: “It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.”
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
articles.title_zh: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "open" to the possibility of the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out considering financial reparations.
Burham said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected by the slave trade" and was open to "calls for an apology".
He dismissed the idea of paying financial reparations, saying they were "not the right answer".
The comments come ahead of a Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean next week, which Burnham will attend. Caribbean nations have renewed calls for the UK to apologise for its role in the slave trade, and for reparations, as King Charles III tours the region .
Burham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in his piece for the Guardian .
He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation". Burnham said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue" adding:   "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."
A government source told the BBC this was "morally the right thing to do".
Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest  to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.
Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.
Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.
Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough.
"The British Government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now. This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice," he said.
From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.
Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.
As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of their slaves.
The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

articles.title_orig: Fake US voters? China-linked accounts flood X with divisive posts ahead of midterms
articles.title_zh: Fake US voters? China-linked accounts flood X with divisive posts ahead of midterms
articles.content_orig:
Fabricated political polling has forced its way into the spotlight during the midterm election period in the United States.
Revelations that a small number of fraudulent firms have released fictitious results – some of which were picked up by news outlets and polling trackers – have raised concerns about how easily false information can acquire credibility.
Those datasets can be used to cast doubt on the electoral process. And when bad actors are unmasked, their existence can be leveraged to undermine voter confidence in election information overall.
The latest example occurred earlier this month, when Wedgewood Polls released a statement on social media admitting its statistics about a bevy of battleground states – like Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Kansas and Maine – were fake.
Wedgewood described its work as “an experimental project” designed to highlight the “vulnerabilities, lack of oversight and overall low barrier to entry” in the US polling industry.
“Having previously worked in the polling and research sector, we watched as the public’s trust in polling eroded alongside a rise in unverified, low-quality methodology,” the firm said in a statement posted to its social media account, which has now been deleted.
It justified its false data as a test to see how easy it would be for fabricated polling to gain traction among voters and the media.
“The short answer: Far too easy,” Wedgewood said.
But Wedgewood’s admission came after its surveys had already circulated through the political information ecosystem, reaching prominent media outlets like The New York Times.
The incident was the second such scandal in the 2026 election cycle, following the exposure of another operation, Median Strategies, which acknowledged in August it had also faked results as a “short-term social experiment”.
In an increasingly polarised US political environment, the incidents have roiled a polling industry – and a public – struggling to adapt to an ever-changing information landscape.
Wedgewood, which launched in June, published surveys covering competitive races across several states. Its results attracted attention from political campaigns, commentators and organisations that compile polling data.
The New York Times said its polling tracker had listed 15 Wedgewood surveys between June and October. The newspaper subsequently removed them.
In the wake of the scandal, it explained that the firm had answered questions about its personnel, methodology and funding before its results were included.
While the Times said Wedgewood’s surveys were not incorporated into the newspaper’s own presidential approval or national congressional polling averages, the case revealed a vulnerability in the process by which polling information becomes established as credible.
Polling aggregators help journalists and voters make sense of a crowded field of surveys by collecting results from multiple research organisations. Their value depends partly on their ability to distinguish reliable research from poorly conducted or fraudulent work.
Wedgewood’s success in passing some of those checks suggests that transparency on paper is not necessarily proof that research has been conducted as claimed.
According to FiftyPlusOne, a polling and forecasting website that investigated the firm, inconsistencies in the raw data and the technical identifiers associated with survey responses helped raise suspicions about its authenticity.
The investigation prompted Wedgewood to acknowledge that most of its results were fabricated.
Though Wedgewood has denied trying to mislead the public, some pollsters are not convinced, suggesting the group could was up to something more nefarious.
“We were investigating Wedgewood for faking their data,” said data journalist G Elliott Morris, who was involved in FiftyPlusOne’s probe. “They are trying to cover up for their fraud with the ‘we were doing a social experiment’ excuse.”
The consequences of fake polling extend far beyond the polling industry.
Mallory McMorrow, who ran unsuccessfully in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, has argued that a Wedgewood survey showing her support in the single digits damaged her campaign.
McMorrow said the poll left her volunteers demoralised, and journalists repeatedly contacted her to ask whether she should abandon the race.
Donations, she added, also evaporated, with Democratic supporters looking to other campaigns to invest.
In a social media post , McMorrow described the poll from Wedgewood – and another from the firm Mitchell Research and Communications – as a “one-two punch” that “killed her campaign”. She suspended her Senate bid in July.
“By that point, we took a risk and we spend our money. We put our ads up. They were working. But the damage was done. And I was drowned out by outside spending and the narrative that we had completely collapsed,” she wrote.
Experts say McMorrow’s account illustrates a broader problem: Even when a poll does not accurately measure public opinion, its findings can still influence the decisions of people who believe it does.
The Wedgewood controversy demonstrates how fraudulent data can become ammunition in an already polarised political environment.
Researchers at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public tracked how discussion of Wedgewood’s admission spread across social media.
Initially, much of the conversation was concentrated among polling experts and people who followed election data. But the story subsequently gained traction among influential political commentators and partisan accounts.
Some posts focused on the fact that prominent outlets and polling aggregators had listed Wedgewood’s results. Others used the revelation to question polling more broadly, particularly surveys suggesting that Democrats were competitive in closely contested races.
The researchers found the controversy became intertwined with claims that polling was systematically misleading voters or understating support for particular political parties.
“Within 24 hours, the right-wing media ecosystem had succeeded in drawing attention to the story and setting some of the most salient frames: that poll numbers around the midterms, especially poll numbers favoring Democrats, cannot be trusted,” the Center for an Informed Public wrote in its analysis.
President Donald Trump, who has regularly made false claims about US election integrity, seized on the revelations to criticise the Times for including Wedgewood’s surveys in its polling tracker.
“The New York Times got caught,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post . “Everything about The Failing New York Times is ‘ARTIFICIAL’.”
He also suggested the Wedgewood case would help his $15bn defamation suit against the Times.
“Our powerful Lawsuit against them is getting stronger and stronger everyday,” he added.
No laws exist in the US that criminalise fake polls outright.
Some advocacy groups and law scholars have argued that the publication of fake polls constitute commodities and wire fraud, warranting federal prosecution.
“Deterring this sort of fraud before it can happen – and raising awareness of it – is vital,” Tyler Yeargain wrote for the Missouri Law Review in 2020.
He argued that enforcement of election-related laws against fake pollsters has “not been fully utilized”.
“Prosecution would serve a strong federal interest,” he wrote. “The interest at stake is weightier than concerns over how fake polls can shade the accuracy of an academic endeavor in prediction markets. It is instead to deter other wrongdoers, the sort who would weaponize fake polls to manipulate elections.”
Brendan Carr, the head of the Federal Communication Commission (FCC), which regulates broadcasts in the US, said there has been “a significant surge” in fake polls during the 2026 midterms, urging networks not to amplify them. Otherwise, Carr said, they could lose their licence to operate.

articles.title_orig: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
articles.title_zh: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
articles.content_orig:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

articles.title_orig: China’s plenum backs tighter party discipline, a priority for Xi. Here's why it matters
articles.title_zh: China’s plenum backs tighter party discipline, a priority for Xi. Here's why it matters
articles.content_orig:
This is the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Since then, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", Zhang Fuhai, from the party's disciplinary commission, told a press briefing on Friday.
He also said the party would enhance its efforts to ensure officials "dare not, cannot, and do not want to be corrupt".
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
The party says it's going after "pointless formalities", which inlcude "bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance"
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violated [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased emphasis on discipline â which many interpret as loyalty â is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder of Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.

President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, returning to Warsaw to deal with the turmoil at home
Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, as riot police deployed around the country’s constitutional court on Friday following the suspension of its chief justice in a battle between the centrist government and the nationalist right.
Dozens of police guarded the entrance to the court as followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) protested against the ousting of constitutional court president Bogdan Swieczkowski.
The court’s official social media account said there had been a “coup d’etat” and some demonstrators chanted “Tusk traitor”, as they condemned the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran wants to talk, predicts conflict will end 'very soon'
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran wants to talk, predicts conflict will end 'very soon'
articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil caught fire Friday after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said, according to state media.
It was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after using unauthorized routes through the strait, the Guard said, according to The Associated Press.
Tehran has repeatedly said vessels must receive permission before traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran warned last month that vessels traveling through the strait without permission risked "destruction."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Friday with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud to discuss regional issues, including Iran, Sudan and Yemen, the State Department said.
They met on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta.
"They discussed bilateral cooperation on a number of regional issues, including in Iran, Sudan, and Yemen," the State Department said in a statement.
"Secretary Rubio also signed the Expo 2030 participation contract, formalizing U.S. participation in Expo 2030 Riyadh, where we will showcase American innovation, expand opportunities for U.S. businesses, and strengthen our partnership with Saudi Arabia," the statement added.
Iran's political establishment is showing signs of divisions over how to end the country's prolonged conflict with the U.S. and Israel as diplomatic efforts intensify, according to Iran International .
Reformist and moderate figures have pushed for renewed negotiations with Washington, while conservatives and hardliners have emphasized military deterrence and maintaining Tehran's demands, the outlet reported.
The debate follows a reported call from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to end the war, while maintaining that any agreement must meet Iran's conditions, according to Iran International.
President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for negotiations, arguing that prolonged uncertainty is hurting Iran's economy.
Hardliners, meanwhile, have argued that Tehran should strengthen its military position and economic resilience.
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Friday that President Donald Trump has been "very upfront" with Americans about the impact the war with Iran is having on fuel prices , calling the increase a "short-term consequence."
"If you also look at what the president has done for our energy industry, he is bringing down the price of gasoline and diesel," Leavitt said during an appearance on "The Story with Martha MacCallum."
"Of course, he's been very upfront with voters in Iowa and all across the country about what the war in Iran is doing," she said. "It's a short-term consequence. But overall, his energy policy will bring gas prices and diesel costs down again."
Leavitt contrasted Trump's energy agenda with Democrats' policies.
"If you look at it in contrast to what the Democrats want to do, they want to completely shut down and phase out our country from fossil fuels, which will jack up energy costs, which will not be good for anyone in rural America or anywhere in America," she said.
Yemen's government said Friday that Iran-aligned Houthis launched ballistic missile attacks targeting Aden International Airport and the presidential palace complex in the city.
A spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces said the Houthis targeted the airport and the Maashiq presidential palace complex, according to Reuters.
Officials did not immediately provide details on casualties or damage, or say whether the missiles struck their intended targets.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Streamer Hasan Piker compared pro-Israel Jewish voters in Michigan to the Ku Klux Klan during a livestream Thursday.
Piker made the comparison while discussing campaign volunteers for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed canvassing a Jewish neighborhood outside Detroit.
He called it "the wildest door-knocking operation of all time," saying volunteers were trying to convince "one of the more Zionist, wealthy districts in the country to vote for a Muslim anti-Zionist."
"Brave soldiers — all of 'em," Piker said.
“This is the equivalent of going to that, like, Klan, KKK neighborhood to stump for like a Black candidate,” he said. “... The supremacist attitude underlying in their worldview is identical.”
He added, “If you are pro-Israel to the degree that you are making a big fuss about never voting for Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim anti-Zionist, yes, it is the equivalent. ... It’s racial supremacy. It’s Jewish supremacy.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Friday that ongoing global crises threaten energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation as G20 foreign ministers gathered in Atlanta.
"We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together with one another to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests," Rubio said in opening remarks, according to Reuters.
"We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle."
The meeting comes as the ongoing war with Iran has raised concerns about global energy supplies and shipping.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Germany's Foreign Office said Friday that most G20 nations agree that Iran must return to negotiations.
"Most of the [G20] share our view: [Iran] must come to the negotiating table, the [Houthis] must cease their attacks, and [Russia] must stop driving global [food security] towards collapse with its attacks in the Black Sea," the account wrote on X.
The statement came as G20 nations gathered amid heightened tensions in the Middle East.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Iran wants "to talk" as the war stretches into its eighth month.
"They want to talk. They keep talking," Trump told reporters.
The president claimed that Iran is struggling to pay its security forces as the conflict continues.
"Look, they're not paying their soldiers, they're not paying their police. They're, you know, they're in a lot of trouble," he said.
The president also described the conflict as "not a typical war" and said Washington is spending "very little money, relatively speaking."
Trump also defended the cost of the U.S. campaign, saying the money was spent "in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon," while arguing U.S. actions in Venezuela have more than offset the expense.
"Any money we've spent in Iran, we've more than made up for with what we did in Venezuela," he said.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on Friday again warned Americans in Saudi Arabia to exercise extreme caution around airports amid ongoing Houthi attacks and travel disruptions.
In its latest security alert, the embassy reiterated that non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members were ordered to leave Saudi Arabia effective Oct. 23 due to "safety risks."
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh wrote on X.
U.S. citizens were also warned of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
"Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia," the post added.
October saw the highest number of reported maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz region since the U.S.-Iran conflict began , according to data released by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
The UKMTO report shows incidents across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman climbed to their highest monthly level in October, with 144 total events reported since Feb. 28.
